title: Figurative Language in Scholarly and Literary Discourse
learningObjectives: Analyze sophisticated phrasal verbs in scholarly writing
Understand literary and philosophical idioms at near-native level
Evaluate the rhetorical function of figurative language
Deploy phrasal verbs and idioms with native-like precision

sections.title: Mastery of Figurative Language
sections.content: At the C2 level, figurative language is not merely decorative — it is a precision instrument for intellectual discourse. Phrasal verbs and idioms in academic, literary, and philosophical writing carry layers of meaning that require deep cultural and linguistic competence. This reading explores how mastery-level English deploys these tools.

sections.title: Phrasal Verbs in Philosophical Writing
sections.content:
Philosophical discourse employs phrasal verbs with precision:

The philosopher grappled with the aporia, seeking to tease out implications of categorical imperatives while pushing back against reductive epistemology. Her work drew on heteroglossia to open up new avenues, ultimately doing away with the vicious circularity of previous arguments.

• <Grapple with> - struggle intellectually with difficulty
• <Tease out> - carefully extract subtle elements
• <Push back against> - resist or challenge
• <Draw on> - use as resource or influence
• <Open up> - create new possibilities
• <Do away with> - eliminate or abolish
• <Arrive at> - reach through reasoning

sections.title: Idioms in Literary Criticism
sections.content:
Literary criticism employs idioms bridging the scholarly and evocative:

• <Read between the lines> - The subaltern narrative requires us to <read between the lines> of colonial texts.
• <A far cry from> - This palimpsest is a far cry from surface-level interpretation.
• <Strike a chord> - The ekphrasis <strikes a chord> across cultures.
• <Cut to the chase> - The topology of the argument is fundamentally flawed.
• <The jury is still out> - No conclusion on whether qualia can be empirically studied.
• <A tall order> - Reconciling inviolability with jurisprudence is <a tall order>.

sections.title: Mastery-Level Usage
sections.content:
Example 1: <The scholar teased out heteroglossia embedded in the palimpsest, drawing on postcolonial theory to push back against essentialist readings.>

Example 2: <The pathophysiology opened up new research avenues, though the requisite interdisciplinary approach proved a tall order.>

Example 3: <Grappling with the aporia of free will, the philosopher arrived at a position doing away with compatibilist circularity.>

sections.title: The Rhetorical Power of Figurative Language
sections.content:
Understanding why a writer chooses a phrasal verb matters as much as what it means:

<Tease out> implies patience — handling fragile ideas.
<Push back against> implies courage — challenging authority.
<Grapple with> implies honest struggle — acknowledging difficulty.
<Do away with> implies decisive action — making a bold claim.

These choices signal the writer's stance, confidence, and relationship to material.

sections.title: Cognitive Metaphor and Conceptual Frameworks
sections.content:
At C2, figurative language requires <cognitive linguistics> and <conceptual metaphor> theory.

Lakoff and Johnson showed metaphor is a cognitive mechanism. ARGUMENT IS WAR: we <attack> positions, <defend> claims, <shoot down> arguments.

• <Dead metaphors> — forgotten figurative origins. We <grasp> concepts, <see> points, <weigh> options without awareness of physical metaphors underneath.
• <Catachresis> — deliberate misuse of metaphor as rhetorical device. Derrida argued all language is catachrestic.

Mastery means recognizing how figurative language shapes thought itself.

sections.title: Figurative Language at Mastery Level
sections.content:
Example 1: ACADEMIC - <The argument falls apart under scrutiny. She glosses over counterexamples and papers over theoretical cracks with rhetorical flourish rather than evidence.>

Example 2: LITERARY - <Woolf's prose doesn't describe consciousness — it enacts it. Sentences ebb, circle back, and branch into tributaries, mirroring the stream of consciousness they capture.>

Example 3: PHILOSOPHICAL - <To "grasp" a concept invokes a bodily metaphor privileging tactile engagement. Our language for abstraction betrays inescapable embodiment — we cannot think our way out of the body that thinks.>

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.content:
Remember:

• C2 figurative language carries rhetorical and philosophical weight
• Phrasal verbs in scholarly writing signal intellectual stance
• Literary idioms bridge analytical precision and evocative power
• The choice of figurative language reveals the writer's relationship to their subject
• Mastery means not just understanding but deploying these tools strategically

keyVocabulary.definition: To struggle intellectually with a complex problem
keyVocabulary.example: Philosophers grapple with questions of consciousness.

keyVocabulary.definition: To carefully extract or identify subtle elements
keyVocabulary.example: The critic teased out hidden themes in the novel.

keyVocabulary.definition: To resist or challenge an idea or authority
keyVocabulary.example: Scholars push back against reductive interpretations.

keyVocabulary.definition: To use something as a resource or influence
keyVocabulary.example: The theory draws on multiple disciplines.
The new framework does away with outdated assumptions.

keyVocabulary.definition: To understand the implicit or hidden meaning
keyVocabulary.example: You need to read between the lines of the report.
This analysis is a far cry from simplistic readings.

keyVocabulary.definition: No definitive conclusion has been reached
keyVocabulary.example: The jury is still out on this theory.

grammarPoints.explanation: At the C2 level, phrasal verbs are chosen not just for meaning but for rhetorical effect.
commonMistakes: Using neutral verbs when a phrasal verb would add rhetorical power to academic writing
